children: Anthropic's economics team has released an interactive model estimating how artificial intelligence could reshape the U.S. economy by 2030.

Built with economists including Anton Korinek and Chad Jones, the model treats every job as a bundle of discrete tasks that AI can automate, augment, leave untouched or supplement with entirely new work.
The team lays out three scenarios.

, AI's economic footprint resembles the internet's: GDP ends up just 1.6% above a no-AI baseline, and unemployment stays within normal historical ranges — a low-conviction case for any AI-driven re-rating of the broader market.
assumes AI autonomously handles about half of all knowledge work by 2030, pushing GDP 8.3% above baseline to $36T (versus roughly $31T today), while total unemployment settles around 4.6%.

Wages overall rise 2.1%, but that gain is unevenly split: knowledge workers see pay edge down 0.3%, while workers in other occupations gain 5.9%. Labor's overall share of GDP slips to 56.1 cents on the dollar, down from 60 cents today, with the remaining 43.9 cents flowing to capital — a split investors weighing equities against labor-sensitive plays should watch.

If AI becomes more productive than humans across nearly all knowledge-work tasks and recursive self-improvement drives rapid adoption, annual GDP growth could hit 15%, doubling the economy roughly every 4.5 years and lifting GDP 32% above baseline to $44.4T.

But the gains would be lopsided: knowledge-worker unemployment would climb well past typical recessionary levels, those workers' wages could fall more than 10%, and capital's share of GDP would jump nearly 15 points to 55%.

That capital-labor split shows up across all three scenarios, not just the extreme one. Even where average wages rise overall, the report finds the increase concentrated outside knowledge work — in construction and other trades that benefit from AI-driven productivity gains elsewhere — while a growing share of total output flows to capital owners rather than paychecks. For income investors
, that's a structural tailwind for capital returns relative to wage growth, regardless of which scenario plays out.

Anthropic also surveyed more than 10K Americans in August to gauge sentiment; the median response lines up closest to the Substantial scenario, while about one in ten respondents held views consistent with the extreme case.

The firm describes the tool as version 1.0 and still incomplete, excluding factors like business-cycle swings, policy responses, and humanoid robotics, but says it will guide the interventions and policy proposals Anthropic funds going forward.
